summary.text: For odd primes, Fermat’s theorem makes \(2^j\) periodic modulo \(p\) with period \(p-1\), and shifting the summation index by \(2(p-1)\) changes the triangular exponent by a multiple of \(p-1\), so the shifted tail matches the original sum. The extra initial terms vanish because each product contains \(2^{p-1}-1\) or \(2^{2(p-1)}-1\), while modulo \(2\) every term except the \(k=0\) term vanishes.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
E(k)=\frac{k(k+1)}2=\binom{k+1}{2}
\]
and, for \(0\le k<N\), let
\[
T_N(k)=2^{E(k)}\prod_{j=k+1}^{N-1}(2^j-1).
\]
As usual, a product over an empty index set is \(1\). Then the sequence in question is
\[
a(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}T_N(k).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

We first dispose of the prime \(p=2\). If \(N\ge 1\), the summand with \(k=0\) is
\[
T_N(0)=2^{E(0)}\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}(2^j-1)
       =\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}(2^j-1).
\]
Every factor \(2^j-1\), for \(j\ge 1\), is odd, so this summand is congruent to \(1\pmod 2\). For every \(k\ge 1\), one has \(E(k)=k(k+1)/2>0\), and hence \(2^{E(k)}\) is even. Thus all the other summands are congruent to zero modulo \(2\). Consequently
\[
a(N)\equiv 1\pmod 2
\]
for every \(N\ge 1\). Since both \(n\) and \(n+2(2-1)=n+2\) are at least \(1\), this gives
\[
a(n+2)\equiv a(n)\pmod 2.
\]

It remains to consider an odd prime \(p\). Put
\[
q=p-1,
\qquad L=2q=2(p-1).
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). Fermat's little theorem therefore gives
\[
2^q=2^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]
It follows more generally that, for all nonnegative integers \(e,t\),
\[
2^{e+qt}=2^e(2^q)^t\equiv 2^e\pmod p. \tag{1}
\]
In particular,
\[
2^{2q+j}\equiv 2^j\pmod p \tag{2}
\]
for every \(j\ge 0\), and also
\[
2^{2q}=(2^q)^2\equiv 1\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]

We compare the summands defining \(a(n+2q)\) with those defining \(a(n)\). There are two parts: the initial indices \(0\le k<2q\), and the remaining indices \(2q\le k<2q+n\).

First we show that every summand in the initial part vanishes modulo \(p\). Fix \(k<2q\). If \(k<q\), then the index \(j=q\) lies in the product range
\[
k+1\le j\le n+2q-1.
\]
Indeed, \(k+1\le q\), and \(q\le n+2q-1\) because \(n\ge 1\) and \(q>0\). The product in \(T_{n+2q}(k)\) therefore contains the factor
\[
2^q-1\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
Hence \(T_{n+2q}(k)\equiv0\pmod p\).

On the other hand, if \(q\le k<2q\), then the index \(j=2q\) lies in that product range: from \(k<2q\) we have \(k+1\le2q\), while
\[
2q\le n+2q-1
\]
because \(n\ge1\). This time the product contains the factor
\[
2^{2q}-1\equiv0\pmod p
\]
by (3). Thus again \(T_{n+2q}(k)\equiv0\pmod p\). We have proved
\[
T_{n+2q}(k)\equiv0\pmod p
\quad\text{for every }0\le k<2q. \tag{4}
\]

Next we prove that each remaining summand is a shifted copy of a summand of \(a(n)\). Every index in the remaining range can be written uniquely as
\[
k=2q+r,
\qquad 0\le r<n.
\]
We claim that
\[
T_{n+2q}(2q+r)\equiv T_n(r)\pmod p. \tag{5}
\]

For the power of \(2\) at the beginning of the summand, a direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(2q+r)
 &=\frac{(2q+r)(2q+r+1)}2\\
 &=\frac{r(r+1)}2+q(2r+2q+1)\\
 &=E(r)+q(2r+2q+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (1), with \(e=E(r)\) and \(t=2r+2q+1\), yields
\[
2^{E(2q+r)}\equiv2^{E(r)}\pmod p. \tag{6}
\]

For the product part, its indices are
\[
2q+r+1\le j\le n+2q-1.
\]
Writing \(j=2q+s\) translates this range bijectively into
\[
r+1\le s\le n-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\prod_{j=2q+r+1}^{n+2q-1}(2^j-1)
=
\prod_{s=r+1}^{n-1}(2^{2q+s}-1).
\]
By (2), every corresponding factor satisfies
\[
2^{2q+s}-1\equiv2^s-1\pmod p.
\]
Multiplying these congruences gives
\[
\prod_{j=2q+r+1}^{n+2q-1}(2^j-1)
\equiv
\prod_{s=r+1}^{n-1}(2^s-1)
\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]
This also covers the case \(r=n-1\), when both products are empty and equal to \(1\). Multiplying (6) and (7) proves (5).

We can now split the full sum defining \(a(n+2q)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n+2q)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n+2q-1}T_{n+2q}(k)\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{2q-1}T_{n+2q}(k)
  +\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}T_{n+2q}(2q+r).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (4), the first sum is zero modulo \(p\). By (5), the second sum is congruent term by term to
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}T_n(r)=a(n).
\]
Hence
\[
a(n+2q)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Finally, \(2q=2(p-1)\), so this is precisely
\[
\boxed{a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p}.
\]
Together with the separate argument for \(p=2\), this proves the assertion for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\ge1\).
